cmp.en: Here śūnya is used in its everyday sense, “lacking something inside”: the cause does not contain the effect. The English “empty of the effect” is literal; it is related to, but not quite the same as, the book's “emptiness.”

verses.en: A non-empty effect will not arise; what is non-empty will not cease. That non-empty thing will be unceasing and unarisen.
How will something empty arise? How will something empty cease? It follows that the empty too is unceasing and unarisen.
It never makes sense for cause and effect to be one. It never makes sense for cause and effect to be different.
If cause and effect were one, producer and produced would be one. If cause and effect were separate, a cause would be the same as a non-cause.
If the effect really existed by own-nature, what would the cause produce? If the effect did not exist by own-nature, what would the cause produce?
Something that is not producing cannot be a cause. And if being a cause makes no sense, whose effect will the effect be?
This assembly of causes and conditions does not produce itself by itself. How could it produce an effect?
So the effect is not made by the assembly, nor made by a non-assembly. Without an effect, where is the assembly of conditions?

chapters.title: Chapter 21 · Examining Coming to Be and Passing Away (Saṃbhavavibhavaparīkṣā)

verses.en: Passing away does not exist, whether apart from coming to be or together with it. Coming to be does not exist, whether apart from passing away or together with it.

cmp.note: 「出现、生起」与「消散、消失」，两词同根，只差前缀。英文 coming to be / passing away 保住了成对的感觉；罗什「成 / 坏」。
cmp.en: Saṃbhava, “coming into being,” and vibhava, “dissolving, disappearing”: the same root with different prefixes. The English “coming to be / passing away” keeps the pairing; Kumārajīva has 成 / 坏 (chéng / huài, “forming / breaking”).

verses.en: How could there be passing away without coming to be? That would be like death without birth. There is no passing away without coming to be.
How could passing away exist together with coming to be? Birth and death do not happen at the same time.
How could there be coming to be without passing away? For impermanence is never absent from things.
How could coming to be exist together with passing away? Birth and death do not happen at the same time.

cmp.note: 这一颂和第 3 颂几乎一样，只是对调了两词。罗什本没有这一颂。英文照梵本译出。
cmp.en: This verse is almost identical to verse 3 with the two terms swapped. Kumārajīva's version lacks it; the English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Two things that cannot be established either together or apart from each other — how on earth can they be established at all?

cmp.note: 「成立、站得住」，是论证用语，和品名的「生成」无关。英文用 established，和 coming to be 分开；罗什都用「成」字，两层意思混了。
cmp.en: Siddhi, “being established, holding up,” is a term of argument, unrelated to “coming to be” in the title. The English keeps them apart with “established”; Kumārajīva uses 成 (chéng) for both, blurring them.

verses.en: What is wasting away has no coming to be, and what is not wasting away has no coming to be. What is wasting away has no passing away, and what is not wasting away has no passing away.
Coming to be and passing away do not exist without a thing. A thing does not exist without coming to be and passing away.
Coming to be and passing away make no sense for what is empty. Coming to be and passing away make no sense for what is not empty.
It makes no sense that coming to be and passing away are one. It makes no sense that coming to be and passing away are different.
You may think coming to be and passing away are plainly seen. But coming to be and passing away are seen out of delusion.

An existent thing is not born from an existent thing; an existent thing is not born from a nonexistent one. A nonexistent thing is not born from a nonexistent one; a nonexistent thing is not born from an existent one.

cmp.note: 「存在的东西 / 不存在」。英文 existent / nonexistent thing 照译；罗什「法 / 非法」容易和「正法 / 非法」（对错）混淆。
cmp.en: “Existent thing / nonexistence.” The English follows it; Kumārajīva's 法 / 非法 (fǎ / fēifǎ) is easily confused with “right / wrong Dharma.”

verses.en: An existent thing is not born from itself, nor from something else, nor from itself and something else together. From where is it born?
For one who accepts existent things, the views of permanence and annihilation follow, since such a thing would have to be either permanent or impermanent.
[An objector:] For one who accepts existent things there is neither annihilation nor permanence, because becoming is the continuum of the rising and falling of effects and causes.

cmp.note: bhava「有、存在、生命的延续」，和 bhāva「存在的东西」只差一个长音。英文把 bhava 译成 becoming，跟 existent thing 分开。这一颂是对方的反驳，梵文没有标记，英文加了 [An objector]。
cmp.en: Bhava, “becoming, the ongoing process of life,” differs from bhāva, “existent thing,” only by a vowel length. The English renders bhava as “becoming” to keep it apart. This verse is the opponent's rejoinder, unmarked in the Sanskrit; the English adds [An objector].

verses.en: If becoming is the continuum of the rising and falling of effects and causes, then since what has fallen away does not arise again, the cause would be cut off.
For what exists by own-nature, it makes no sense to become nonexistent. And at the time of nirvana there would be annihilation, since the stream of becoming has come to rest.
It makes no sense that the first becoming begins when the last has ceased. Nor does it make sense that the first begins when the last has not ceased.

cmp.note: 「最后的有」与「最初的有」：这一世的最后一刻和下一世的第一刻。英文 the last / the first 照字面，读者需要知道这是在讲投生。
cmp.en: “The last becoming” and “the first becoming”: the last moment of this life and the first moment of the next. The English “the last / the first” is literal; readers should know this is about rebirth.

verses.en: If the first is born while the last is ceasing, then one would be ceasing and another would be arising.
And if it makes no sense that what is ceasing and what is arising are separate, then one would be born in the very aggregates in which one is dying at that same moment.

cmp.note: 梵文前半句很简略，主语和省略的成分不确定。英文和白话各补了一种读法，罗什的「生灭一时」与白话理解相同；英文的补法是「正在灭的和正在生的是分开的」，结论都一样：人在死去的同一组蕴里出生。
cmp.en: The first line is very terse, and the subject and what is left out are uncertain. The English and plain Chinese each fill it in; the plain Chinese, like Kumārajīva's 生灭一时 (“arising and ceasing at one time”), supplies “simultaneous,” while the English supplies “separate.” Both reach the same conclusion: one would be born in the same aggregates one dies in.

verses.en: So in none of the three times does the stream of becoming make sense. And what does not exist in any of the three times — how can it be a stream of becoming?
The Tathagata is not the aggregates, nor other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them; nor does he possess the aggregates. Then which one here is the Tathagata?

cmp.note: 佛的称号，可以拆成 tathā-gata「如此而去的」或 tathā-āgata「如此而来的」。英文保留原词 Tathagata（全书不加变音符号），中文「如来」只取了「来」这一种拆法。
cmp.en: A title of the Buddha that can be split as tathā-gata, “thus gone,” or tathā-āgata, “thus come.” The English keeps the word “Tathagata” (without diacritics throughout); the Chinese 如来 (rúlái, “thus come”) takes only the “come” reading.

cmp.note: 这就是第 16 品第 2 颂说的「五种方式」：是蕴、异于蕴、蕴在他里、他在蕴里、拥有蕴。罗什压成「非阴不离阴，此彼不相在」，又把「不同」说成「不离」。
cmp.en: These are the “five ways” mentioned in chapter 16, verse 2: being the aggregates, being other than them, having them in him, being in them, possessing them. Kumārajīva compresses them, and renders “not other than” as 不离 (bù lí, “not apart from”).

verses.en: If the Buddha exists in dependence on the aggregates, he does not exist by own-nature. And what does not exist by own-nature — how could it exist by other-nature?
Whatever exists in dependence on other-nature can rightly be called selfless. And how could what is selfless be the Tathagata?
If there is no own-nature, how could there be other-nature? Apart from own-nature and other-nature, who is the Tathagata?
If there were some Tathagata without depending on the aggregates, he would now take them up, and having taken them up, he would then exist.

cmp.note: 「依靠、取着」：和第 8、16、18 品的「执取」是同一个词。这一品英文译 depend on / take up / what is taken up，好让「如来依靠五蕴」读得通；读者要知道它和 grasping 是同一个梵文词。
cmp.en: “Depending on, taking up”: the same word as “grasping” in chapters 8, 16 and 18. In this chapter the English uses “depend on / take up / what is taken up” so that “the Tathagata depends on the aggregates” reads naturally; readers should know it is the same Sanskrit word as “grasping.”

verses.en: But without depending on the aggregates there is no Tathagata at all. And how will what does not exist without depending take anything up?
There is no taking up without something taken up. And there is in no way a Tathagata without taking up.

cmp.note: 这里 upādāna 可以指「依靠的动作」，也可以指「被依靠的东西」。英文 taking up / something taken up 把两义拆开写；梵文是一个词。
cmp.en: Here upādāna can mean the act of taking up or the thing taken up. The English separates them as “taking up / something taken up”; the Sanskrit uses one word.

verses.en: He who is not found as the same or as different, when sought in the five ways — how is that Tathagata designated by what he takes up?

cmp.note: 「被施设、被称呼」：能不能凭五蕴给如来安一个名字。英文 designated；罗什改成「受中有」，问的是有没有，少了「安名」这一层。
cmp.en: “Is designated, is named”: can the Tathagata be given a name on the basis of the aggregates? The English says “designated”; Kumārajīva's 受中有 (“is he present in what is taken up?”) asks about existence and loses the naming.

verses.en: And this that is taken up does not exist by own-nature. And what does not exist by own-nature — how could it exist by other-nature?
So what is taken up and the one who takes up are empty in every way. How can an empty Tathagata be designated by something empty?

cmp.note: 后半句可以读成反问（说不出来），也可以读成「正是这样被称说」。英文和罗什都作反问。
cmp.en: The second line can be read as a rhetorical question (he cannot be designated) or as “that is exactly how he is designated.” The English, like Kumārajīva, takes it as a question.

verses.en: One should not say “empty,” nor “not empty,” nor “both,” nor “neither.” But they are spoken for the sake of designation.

cmp.note: 「施设」：为了说明而方便安立的名称。英文全书译 designation；罗什「假名」的「假」是「借来用」，不是「虚假」。
cmp.en: Prajñapti, a name put in place for the sake of communication. Throughout, the English says “designation”; in Kumārajīva's 假名 (jiǎmíng), 假 means “borrowed,” not “fake.”

verses.en: How could the four — permanent, impermanent and so on — apply to this peaceful one? How could the four — finite, infinite and so on — apply to this peaceful one?

cmp.note: 「四句」：是、不是、又是又不是、既不是是也不是不是。这里指佛不回答的那些问题：世界常不常、有没有边。英文 the four 照字面；罗什加了「相」。
cmp.en: “The four”: is, is not, both, neither. Here they are the questions the Buddha left unanswered: is the world permanent, is it finite. The English “the four” is literal; Kumārajīva adds 相 (xiàng, “mark”).

verses.en: Whoever has seized the heavy grasp “the Tathagata exists” will imagine “he does not exist,” conceptualizing even about one who has gone to nirvana.

cmp.note: 「厚重的抓取」。英文 heavy grasp 照字面；罗什译「邪见深厚」，又漏了「先执著有」这个环节。
cmp.en: “A dense grasp.” The English “heavy grasp” is literal; Kumārajīva's 邪见深厚 (“deep in wrong views”) also drops the step “first clinging to ‘he exists.’”

verses.en: Since he is empty by own-nature, the thought that the Buddha exists or does not exist after his cessation makes no sense at all.
Those who proliferate concepts about the Buddha, who is beyond conceptual proliferation and imperishable — all of them, struck down by conceptual proliferation, do not see the Tathagata.

cmp.note: avyaya「不会消失的」，罗什没有译；「被戏论所伤」，罗什加了「破慧眼」的比喻。英文两处都照梵文。
cmp.en: Avyaya, “imperishable,” is left out by Kumārajīva; for “struck down by conceptual proliferation” he adds the image 破慧眼 (“destroys the eye of wisdom”). The English follows the Sanskrit in both places.

verses.en: Whatever nature the Tathagata has, that is the nature of this world. The Tathagata has no own-nature; this world has no own-nature.
Desire, hatred and delusion are said to spring from mental construction, for they arise in dependence on the attractive, the unattractive, and the distortions.

cmp.note: 「美好、可爱」与「不美好、可厌」。英文 attractive / unattractive，白话「美好 / 不美好」；罗什「净 / 不净」偏向干净与污秽。
cmp.en: “Lovely, pleasing” and “unlovely, repulsive.” The English says “attractive / unattractive,” the plain Chinese 美好 / 不美好 (“lovely / not lovely”); Kumārajīva's 净 / 不净 (jìng / bújìng, “pure / impure”) leans toward clean versus filthy.

cmp.note: 「颠倒、看反了」：把无常当常、把苦当乐之类。英文全书译 distortions；中文「颠倒」（倒过来）的意象更鲜明。
cmp.en: Viparyāsa, “inversion, getting it backwards”: taking the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, and so on. Throughout, the English says “distortions”; the Chinese 颠倒 (diāndǎo, “upside down”) has the more vivid image.

verses.en: What arises in dependence on the attractive, the unattractive and the distortions does not exist by own-nature. So the afflictions are not real.
The existence or nonexistence of the self cannot be established in any way. Without it, how can the existence or nonexistence of the afflictions be established?
For these afflictions belong to someone, and that someone is not established. Or if they exist without anyone, they belong to no one.

Like the view of one's own body as self, the afflictions are not in the afflicted one in any of the five ways. Like the view of one's own body as self, the afflicted one is not in the afflictions in any of the five ways either.

cmp.note: 「身见」：把身心五蕴当成自我的看法。英文 the view of one's own body as self 把意思展开了；罗什又只译了一个方向，漏了「在烦恼里也找不到被染污者」。
cmp.en: “The view of one's own body (as self)”: taking the five aggregates to be a self. The English spells this out; Kumārajīva translates only one direction and drops “the afflicted one is not found in the afflictions.”

verses.en: The attractive, the unattractive and the distortions do not exist by own-nature. So in dependence on which attractive, unattractive and distortions do the afflictions arise?
Form, sound, taste, touch, smell and mental objects — these six are imagined as the basis of desire, hatred and delusion.

cmp.note: 「被分别、被想象成」：这六种只是被心想成了三毒的对象。英文 imagined as 照译；罗什直接说「是三毒根本」，少了「被想象」这一层。
cmp.en: “Are imagined as”: these six are only constructed by the mind into objects of the three poisons. The English keeps “imagined”; Kumārajīva says flatly they “are the root of the three poisons,” losing that layer.

verses.en: Form, sound, taste, touch, smell and mental objects are nothing but things like a city of the gandharvas, like a mirage, like a dream.

cmp.note: 「仅仅是」。梵文这里没有「空」字。英文 nothing but 照译；罗什加了「皆空」。
cmp.en: “Merely.” There is no word “empty” here. The English “nothing but” follows the Sanskrit; Kumārajīva adds 皆空 (jiē kōng, “all empty”).

verses.en: How could there be anything unattractive or attractive in them, when they are like a magically conjured person, like a reflection?
There is no unattractive that we could designate without depending on the attractive. And the attractive depends on that; so the attractive makes no sense.
There is no attractive that we could designate without depending on the unattractive. And the unattractive depends on that; so the unattractive does not exist.
If the attractive does not exist, where will desire come from? If the unattractive does not exist, where will hatred come from?
If grasping the impermanent as “permanent” is a distortion, then since in the empty there is not even anything impermanent, how is that grasping a distortion?

cmp.note: 「空里面连无常都没有」。英文 not even anything impermanent 照译；罗什写成「空中无有常」（空中没有常），意思不同。
cmp.en: “In the empty there is nothing impermanent.” The English “not even anything impermanent” follows it; Kumārajīva writes 空中无有常 (“in emptiness there is nothing permanent”), a different point.

verses.en: If grasping the impermanent as “permanent” is a distortion, why isn't grasping it as “impermanent” a distortion too, in the empty?
That by which one grasps, the grasping, the grasper and what is grasped — all are at peace. So grasping does not exist.

cmp.note: 这一组颂用的 grāha「抓、执著」和全书的 upādāna 是不同的词。英文都用 grasp 一族，读者不必分；严格说 grāha 更偏「抓住一个看法」。
cmp.en: The grāha (“seizing, clinging”) in these verses is a different word from the book's upādāna. The English uses “grasp” for both and the reader need not distinguish them, though strictly grāha leans toward seizing on a view.

verses.en: And if there is no grasping, false or true, who could have a distortion? Who could be free of distortion?
Distortions do not arise in one who is already distorted. Nor do distortions arise in one who is not distorted.
Distortions do not arise in one who is in the middle of being distorted. Think it over for yourself: in whom do distortions arise?
How can distortions that have not arisen exist? And if distortions are unborn, where is anyone caught in distortion?
A thing is not born from itself, nor from something else, nor from both itself and something else. So where is anyone caught in distortion?

cmp.note: 这一颂把第 1 品「不自生、不他生、不共生」搬到颠倒上。罗什本没有这一颂；英文照梵本译出。
cmp.en: This verse applies chapter 1's “not from itself, not from another, not from both” to the distortions. Kumārajīva's version lacks it; the English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: If self, purity, permanence and happiness really existed, then self, purity, permanence and happiness would not be distortions.
If self, purity, permanence and happiness do not exist, then no-self, impurity, impermanence and suffering do not exist either.

cmp.note: 梵文列了无我、不净、无常、苦四样。英文四样都译；罗什漏了「无我」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit lists four: no-self, impurity, impermanence, suffering. The English keeps all four; Kumārajīva drops “no-self.”

verses.en: In this way, ignorance ceases through the ceasing of the distortions. When ignorance has ceased, volitional formations and the rest cease.
If someone's afflictions really existed by own-nature, how could they be abandoned? Who can abandon an own-nature?
If someone's afflictions did not exist by own-nature, how could they be abandoned? Who can abandon what does not exist?
[An objector:] If all this is empty, there is no arising and no passing away. Then for you it follows that the four noble truths do not exist.

cmp.note: 第 1 到 6 颂是反对者的质问，第 7 颂开头「对此我们回答」才分出两边。英文在这里加了 [An objector]；罗什本没有提示。
cmp.en: Verses 1–6 are the opponent's challenge; “To this we reply” at the start of verse 7 marks the turn. The English adds [An objector] here; Kumārajīva's version gives no signal.

cmp.note: 「圣者的真理」：苦、苦的来源、苦的止息、止息苦的道路。英文 the four noble truths 是通行译法，「noble」原指「圣者的」，不是「高贵的」。
cmp.en: “Truths of the noble ones”: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path to its cessation. The English “the four noble truths” is the standard rendering; “noble” here means “belonging to the noble (awakened) ones,” not “aristocratic.”

verses.en: Full understanding, abandoning, cultivating and realizing make no sense, since the four noble truths do not exist.
Since they do not exist, the four noble fruits do not exist either. With no fruits, there are no people established in the fruits, and no people on the way to them.

cmp.note: 声闻修行的四个果位：入流、一来、不还、阿罗汉。英文 the four noble fruits 照字面，没有展开名目。
cmp.en: The four stages of a disciple's practice: stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. The English “the four noble fruits” is literal and does not list them.

verses.en: If those eight kinds of persons do not exist, there is no Sangha. And since the noble truths do not exist, the true Dharma does not exist either.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「僧团」「正法」。英文 Sangha / the true Dharma 照译；罗什加了「宝」字，先点出三宝。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit just says “community” and “true Dharma.” The English has “Sangha / the true Dharma”; Kumārajīva adds 宝 (bǎo, “jewel”), pointing ahead to the Three Jewels.

verses.en: And if there is no Dharma and no Sangha, how will there be a Buddha? Speaking this way, you undermine all Three Jewels.
You undermine emptiness, the real existence of fruits, non-Dharma and Dharma, and all the everyday conventions of the world.
To this we reply: you do not understand the purpose of emptiness, emptiness itself, or the meaning of emptiness. That is why you are troubled this way.

cmp.note: 三样：空性的用处、空性本身、空性的意思。英文三样都分开译；罗什译「空空因缘」与「空义」，「用处」变成了「因缘」。
cmp.en: Three things: the purpose of emptiness, emptiness itself, and its meaning. The English keeps all three apart; Kumārajīva has 空空因缘 and 空义, turning “purpose” into “the reason for it.”

verses.en: The Buddhas' teaching of the Dharma relies on two truths: the conventional truth of the world, and the truth in the ultimate sense.

cmp.note: saṃvṛti 原义「遮盖」，也有「约定、共识」的意思；英文全书译 conventional truth（中文「世俗谛」），只取了「约定」一义。paramārtha「最高的意义」，英文 ultimate（中文「胜义谛 / 第一义谛」）。
cmp.en: Saṃvṛti originally means “covering,” and also “agreement, convention.” Throughout, the English says “conventional truth” (Chinese 世俗谛, shìsú dì), keeping only the “convention” sense. Paramārtha, “the highest meaning,” is “ultimate” (Chinese 胜义谛 / 第一义谛).

verses.en: Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the deep reality in the Buddha's teaching.
Without relying on everyday language, the ultimate cannot be taught. Without arriving at the ultimate, nirvana is not attained.

cmp.note: 这里用的是 vyavahāra「日常言说」，不是上一颂的 saṃvṛti。英文换成 everyday language；罗什都译「俗谛」。罗什还把「第一义无法被宣说」改成「得不到第一义」。
cmp.en: This verse uses vyavahāra, “everyday usage,” not saṃvṛti from verse 8. The English switches to “everyday language”; Kumārajīva uses 俗谛 for both. He also turns “the ultimate cannot be taught” into “the ultimate cannot be attained.”

verses.en: Emptiness wrongly seen ruins a person of weak understanding, like a snake grabbed the wrong way or a spell cast the wrong way.
That is why the Sage's mind turned back from teaching, knowing how hard this Dharma is for the dull to fathom.

cmp.note: 「心转回去了」：指佛成道后起初不愿说法的传说。英文 mind turned back 照字面；罗什「不欲说」。
cmp.en: “The mind turned back”: the story that after his awakening the Buddha at first hesitated to teach. The English “mind turned back” is literal; Kumārajīva has 不欲说 (“did not wish to teach”).

verses.en: The fault you keep finding with emptiness is no fault that applies to us; it makes no sense for what is empty.

cmp.note: 字义不太确定，大致是「指责、贬低」。英文 the fault you keep finding 是一种推测；罗什理解为「你说我执著空」。
cmp.en: The meaning of adhilaya is uncertain, roughly “censure, disparagement.” The English “the fault you keep finding” is a best guess; Kumārajīva takes it as “you say I am attached to emptiness.”

verses.en: For whom emptiness works, everything works. For whom emptiness does not work, nothing works.
Pinning your own faults on us, you are like someone riding a horse who has forgotten the very horse he is riding.
If you see things as really existing by own-nature, then in that case you see things as having no causes or conditions.
You undermine effect and cause, the doer, the instrument and the act, arising and ceasing, and the fruit.
Dependent arising — that is what we call emptiness. It is a designation that depends on something, and it is the middle way itself.

cmp.note: 主语是「缘起」这个道理本身。英文 Dependent arising — that is… 保住了这一点；罗什换成「众因缘生法」（因缘生出来的东西），白话「凡是缘起的」也有一点往「事物」那边偏。
cmp.en: The subject is dependent arising as such. The English “Dependent arising — that is…” keeps this; Kumārajīva switches to 众因缘生法 (“things produced by causes and conditions”), and the plain Chinese 凡是缘起的 (“whatever arises dependently”) also leans a little toward things.

cmp.note: 「依靠（别的东西）而安立的称呼」，「它」指空性：空性本身也只是一个借来用的名字。英文 a designation that depends on something 照译；罗什「亦为是假名」读起来像在说「因缘生法也是假名」。
cmp.en: “A designation made in dependence,” and “it” is emptiness: emptiness itself is only a borrowed name. The English “a designation that depends on something” follows this; Kumārajīva's 亦为是假名 (“it is also a provisional name”) reads as if the things were the provisional name.

cmp.note: 「中间的道路」：不落「有」也不落「无」。英文 the middle way 是全书书名的来源。后世天台宗把罗什这一颂读成「空、假、中」三谛，梵文没有三分的结构。
cmp.en: “The middle path”: falling into neither “exists” nor “does not exist.” The English “the middle way” is where the book's title comes from. The later Chinese Tiantai school read Kumārajīva's verse as three truths — empty, provisional, middle — a structure the Sanskrit does not have.

verses.en: Since there is no thing at all that has not arisen dependently, there is no thing at all that is not empty.
If all this is not empty, there is no arising and no passing away. Then for you it follows that the four noble truths do not exist.

cmp.note: 和第 1 颂只差一个字：「空」换成「不空」，把对方的质问原样还回去。英文也只改了一个词，让读者看到这个对称。
cmp.en: This differs from verse 1 by a single word, “empty” becoming “not empty,” handing the objection straight back. The English also changes only that word so readers can see the symmetry.

verses.en: How will there be suffering that has not arisen dependently? It was taught that suffering is the impermanent; and that does not exist in what has own-nature.
How could what already exists by own-nature arise all over again? So for one who rejects emptiness, there is no origin of suffering.
There is no cessation of suffering that exists by own-nature. By clinging to own-nature, you reject cessation.
If the path had own-nature, cultivating it would make no sense. But if the path is cultivated, then your own-nature does not exist.

cmp.note: 这一颂的主语是「道」。英文和白话照译；罗什开头沿用了「苦若有定性」，主语变了。
cmp.en: The subject of this verse is the path. The English and plain Chinese follow it; Kumārajīva opens with “if suffering had a fixed nature,” carrying over the previous verses' subject.

verses.en: When suffering, its origin and its cessation do not exist, where will the path lead, as the cessation of suffering?
If by own-nature it is not fully understood, how could it later be fully understood? Isn't own-nature, as you say, fixed?
In the same way, for you, abandoning, realizing and cultivating, and the four fruits too, make no sense, just like full understanding.
For one who holds on to own-nature, how could a fruit that by own-nature has not been attained ever be attained later?
With no fruits, there are no people established in the fruits, and no people on the way to them. If those eight kinds of persons do not exist, there is no Sangha.
And since the noble truths do not exist, the true Dharma does not exist either. If there is no Dharma and no Sangha, how will there be a Buddha?
For you, it follows that a Buddha would exist without depending on awakening, and awakening would exist without depending on a Buddha.
For you, one who by own-nature is not a Buddha will not attain awakening, even striving for it through the bodhisattva's practice.

cmp.note: 「凭自性不是佛的人」，是自性论的推论。英文照译；罗什「先非佛性」容易让人联想到后来如来藏系统的「佛性」，那是另一个概念。
cmp.en: “One who by own-nature is not a Buddha,” an inference from the own-nature view. The English follows it; Kumārajīva's 先非佛性 can make readers think of the later idea of “Buddha-nature,” a different concept.

verses.en: And no one would ever do anything in accord with Dharma or against it. What is there to be done by what is not empty? For own-nature is not something done.
For you, there would be fruit even without Dharma and non-Dharma, and there would be no fruit caused by Dharma and non-Dharma.
Or if for you the fruit is caused by Dharma and non-Dharma, how can that fruit, arisen from Dharma and non-Dharma, be not empty?
You undermine all the everyday conventions of the world when you reject the emptiness that is dependent arising.
For one who rejects emptiness, there would be nothing to be done, action would never get started, and a doer would be one who does nothing.
The world would be unborn and unceasing, frozen in place, stripped of its many different states.

cmp.note: 「像铁砧一样固定不动的」。英文 frozen in place，白话「凝固不动」；罗什「常住而不坏」。
cmp.en: Kūṭastha, “fixed like an anvil.” The English says “frozen in place,” the plain Chinese 凝固不动 (“solidified, unmoving”); Kumārajīva has 常住而不坏 (“ever-abiding and indestructible”).

verses.en: If things were not empty, there would be no attaining what has not been attained, no action that ends suffering, and no abandoning of all afflictions.
Whoever sees dependent arising sees this: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

cmp.note: 梵文没有「见佛」，也没有「经中说」。英文照梵文；罗什把佛经里「见缘起即见法，见法即见佛」一类的话带了进来。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has neither “sees the Buddha” nor “as the sutra says.” The English follows the Sanskrit; Kumārajīva brings in the well-known sutra line “whoever sees dependent arising sees the Dharma; whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha.”

verses.en: [An objector:] If all this is empty, there is no arising and no passing away. Then through the abandoning of what, or the ceasing of what, is nirvana supposed to happen — and for whom?

cmp.note: 梵文问「谁的涅槃」。英文 and for whom 译出了；罗什「何断何所灭」略去了「谁」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit asks “whose nirvana?” The English keeps “and for whom”; Kumārajīva's 何断何所灭 (“what is cut off, what ceases?”) drops the “whose.”

verses.en: [Reply:] If all this is not empty, there is no arising and no passing away. Then through the abandoning of what, or the ceasing of what, is nirvana supposed to happen — and for whom?
Not abandoned, not attained, not cut off, not permanent, not ceased, not arisen: this is called nirvana.

cmp.note: 「没有被舍弃、没有被获得」。英文两样都译；罗什「无得亦无至」都是「获得、到达」一类，漏了「没有被舍弃」。
cmp.en: “Not abandoned, not attained.” The English keeps both; Kumārajīva's 无得亦无至 (“nothing gained, nothing reached”) are both about attaining and drop “not abandoned.”

verses.en: First, nirvana is not an existent thing, or it would follow that it has the marks of aging and death. For there is no existent thing without aging and death.
And if nirvana were an existent thing, nirvana would be conditioned. For nowhere is there any existent thing that is unconditioned.
And if nirvana were an existent thing, how could it be without dependence? For there is no existent thing at all that is without dependence.

cmp.note: 「不依靠」，和「执取」同一个字根。英文 without dependence；罗什「无受」的「受」是「取」，不是「感受」。
cmp.en: “Without depending,” from the same root as “grasping.” The English says “without dependence”; in Kumārajīva's 无受 (wú shòu), 受 means “taking,” not “feeling.”

verses.en: If nirvana is not an existent thing, will it be a nonexistence? Where there is no existent thing, there is no nonexistence either.
And if nirvana were a nonexistence, how could it be without dependence? For there is no nonexistence that exists without dependence.
The state of coming and going, when it depends on things or is conditioned, is taught as nirvana when it does not depend and is not conditioned.

cmp.note: 「来了又去、去了又来」的状态，指生死流转。英文 the state of coming and going 照字面；罗什「轮转生死」。
cmp.en: “The state of coming and going, again and again”: the round of birth and death. The English “the state of coming and going” is literal; Kumārajīva has 轮转生死 (“revolving in birth and death”).

cmp.note: 梵文说同一个东西，依靠时叫轮转，不依靠时叫涅槃。英文保住了这个「同一个东西」；罗什写成执取因缘就轮转、不执取就是涅槃，变成了修行上的因果。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit speaks of one and the same thing, called samsara when dependent and nirvana when not. The English keeps it as one thing; Kumārajīva makes it a cause-and-effect of practice: grasping conditions means samsara, not grasping means nirvana.

verses.en: The Teacher spoke of abandoning both becoming and non-becoming. So it makes sense that nirvana is neither an existent thing nor a nonexistence.

cmp.note: 「生存」与「生存的断绝」，指贪求生存和贪求断灭两种执着。英文 becoming / non-becoming，和全书 bhava 的译法一致；罗什改成「如佛经中说，断有断非有」。
cmp.en: “Becoming” and “the end of becoming,” the two cravings for continued existence and for annihilation. The English “becoming / non-becoming” matches the book's rendering of bhava; Kumārajīva changes “the Teacher” to “as the sutras say.”

verses.en: If nirvana were both a nonexistence and an existent thing, liberation would be both a nonexistence and an existent thing. That makes no sense.
If nirvana were both a nonexistence and an existent thing, nirvana would not be without dependence, since both of these depend on something.
How could nirvana be both a nonexistence and an existent thing? Nirvana is unconditioned, while existence and nonexistence are conditioned.
How could nirvana be both a nonexistence and an existent thing? The two cannot be in one place, like light and darkness.
The claim “nirvana is neither a nonexistence nor an existent thing” would be established only if nonexistence and existence were established.

cmp.note: 「表明（的说法）」，指这句话本身。英文 the claim；罗什「分别」，带出心里区分的意思，又把这一颂和下一颂对调了。
cmp.en: Añjanā, “the statement,” the claim itself. The English says “the claim”; Kumārajīva's 分别 (fēnbié, “discriminating”) brings in mental distinction-making, and he also swaps this verse with the next.

verses.en: If nirvana is neither a nonexistence nor an existent thing, who could make it known that it is “neither a nonexistence nor an existent thing”?

cmp.note: 「由谁表明」：谁能认知、说出这一点。英文 who could make it known；罗什「以何而分别」问的是凭什么。
cmp.en: “By whom is it made known?” — who could know and say this. The English “who could make it known” follows it; Kumārajīva's 以何而分别 asks “by what means,” not “by whom.”

verses.en: After his cessation, the Blessed One cannot be said to exist, nor not to exist, nor both, nor neither.
Even while he remains alive, the Blessed One cannot be said to exist, nor not to exist, nor both, nor neither.
There is not the slightest thing that distinguishes samsara from nirvana. There is not the slightest thing that distinguishes nirvana from samsara.

cmp.note: 梵文是「轮回」。英文 samsara 照译；罗什「世间」（世界）范围看起来更宽。这一颂是全书最常被引用的话之一。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says saṃsāra. The English keeps “samsara”; Kumārajīva's 世间 (shìjiān, “the world”) looks broader. This is one of the most often quoted verses in the book.

verses.en: The limit of nirvana is the limit of samsara. Between the two there is not even the subtlest gap.

cmp.note: 只是「边、端」。英文 limit 照字面；罗什把涅槃那一边译成「实际」，后来在汉语佛教里常指「真实的究竟」，意思比原文重。
cmp.en: Koṭi simply means “edge, end.” The English “limit” is literal; Kumārajīva renders nirvana's side as 实际 (shíjì), which later Chinese Buddhism often read as “ultimate reality,” heavier than the original.

verses.en: The views about what comes after cessation, about whether the world has an end, and about whether it is permanent, rest on nirvana, on the future and on the past.
Since all things are empty, what is endless? What has an end? What is both endless and with an end? What is neither endless nor with an end?
What is the same? What is other? What is permanent? What is impermanent? What is both impermanent and permanent? Or what is neither?
The stilling of all apprehending, the stilling of conceptual proliferation, is peace. No Dharma was ever taught by the Buddha anywhere, to anyone.

cmp.note: 「一切把捉的止息」：心不再去抓取对象。英文 the stilling of all apprehending 照译；罗什「诸法不可得」把主语从心的活动换成了诸法，又漏了 śiva「安稳」。
cmp.en: “The stilling of all apprehending”: the mind no longer seizes on objects. The English follows it; Kumārajīva's 诸法不可得 (“no dharma can be found”) shifts the subject from the mind's activity to things, and he drops śiva, “peace.”

cmp.note: 和第 1 品归敬颂的「戏论平息」首尾呼应。英文用同一个译法 the stilling / calming of conceptual proliferation，让读者看到这个呼应。
cmp.en: This echoes “the calming of conceptual proliferation” in the opening homage of chapter 1. The English uses the same rendering so the reader can hear the echo.

verses.en: Veiled by ignorance, one creates the three kinds of volitional formations for the sake of rebirth, and through these actions goes to a destination.

cmp.note: 「十二支」：缘起的十二个环节，从无明到老死。英文 the twelve links；罗什品名「十二因缘」。
cmp.en: “The twelve limbs”: the twelve links of dependent arising, from ignorance to aging-and-death. The English says “the twelve links”; Kumārajīva's title is 十二因缘 (“the twelve causes and conditions”).

cmp.note: 「去处」，没说是几道。英文 a destination 照字面；罗什点明「六趣」。
cmp.en: Gati, “destination, where one goes,” without saying how many. The English “a destination” is literal; Kumārajīva specifies 六趣 (“the six destinies”).

verses.en: With volitional formations as condition, consciousness settles into that destination. Once consciousness has settled, name-and-form is poured in.

cmp.note: 「进入、安住下来」，像种子落进土里；「被注入」，像种子注入母胎。英文 settles / poured in 照字面；罗什「着」「增长」偏到了「执着」「生长」。
cmp.en: “Enters and settles,” like a seed landing in soil; “is poured in,” like a seed into the womb. The English “settles / poured in” is literal; Kumārajīva's 着 (zhuó, “attaches”) and 增长 (zēngzhǎng, “grows”) drift toward clinging and growth.

cmp.note: 「名色」：心（名）与身（色）。英文 name-and-form 是通行直译，读者需要知道是「心与身」。
cmp.en: Nāmarūpa, “name and form”: mind (name) and body (form). The English “name-and-form” is the standard literal rendering; readers should know it means mind and body.

verses.en: When name-and-form has been poured in, the six sense bases come to be. Coming upon the six sense bases, contact takes place.
In dependence on the eye, visible form and attention — that is, in dependence on name-and-form — consciousness takes place.

cmp.note: 罗什本没有这一颂和下一颂，只在上一颂用「情尘识和合」一句带过。英文照梵本译出。
cmp.en: Kumārajīva's version lacks this verse and the next, covering them with one phrase in the previous verse. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The coming together of the three — visible form, consciousness and the eye — is contact. And from contact, feeling takes place.
With feeling as condition there is craving, for one craves for the sake of feeling. Craving, one takes up the four kinds of grasping.

cmp.note: 梵文还给了理由「因为是为了感受而渴求」。英文和白话译出；罗什没有，又补上「六触」「三受」的分类。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit adds the reason, “for one craves for the sake of feeling.” The English and plain Chinese keep it; Kumārajīva drops it and adds classifications (“six contacts,” “three feelings”) not in the Sanskrit.

verses.en: When there is grasping, the grasper's becoming starts up. If he were without grasping, he would be freed, and there would be no becoming.

cmp.note: 十二支里的「有」：新一轮的生存。英文和第 21 品一样译 becoming；中文「有」字面只是「存在」。
cmp.en: Bhava as a link in the chain: a new round of existence. The English uses “becoming,” as in chapter 21; the Chinese 有 (yǒu) literally just means “existence.”

verses.en: That becoming is the five aggregates. From becoming, birth starts up; then aging-and-death, suffering and the rest, sorrow with lamentation,

cmp.note: 「这『有』就是五蕴」。英文和白话译出；罗什没有，又把忧悲说成从老死而来。
cmp.en: “That becoming is the five aggregates.” The English and plain Chinese keep it; Kumārajīva omits it, and makes sorrow and grief come from aging-and-death.

verses.en: dejection and distress — all this starts up from birth. That is how this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
So the one who does not know creates volitional formations, the root of samsara. The one who does not know is the doer; the one who knows is not, because he sees reality.

cmp.note: 「因为见到真实」。英文和白话译出；罗什没有，句读也把「行是轮回的根」读成了「这就是生死」。
cmp.en: “Because he sees reality.” The English and plain Chinese keep it; Kumārajīva omits it, and his phrasing turns “formations are the root of samsara” into “this is birth and death.”

verses.en: When ignorance has ceased, volitional formations do not arise. And the ceasing of ignorance comes from cultivating this very knowledge.

cmp.note: 罗什本没有这一颂，没讲无明怎样灭。梵文「这个认识」没说明认识的是什么，照上下文是对缘起的认识。
cmp.en: Kumārajīva's version lacks this verse, so it never says how ignorance ends. “This very knowledge” is not specified in the Sanskrit; from context it is knowledge of dependent arising.

verses.en: Through the ceasing of each link, the next does not start up. In this way this entire mass of suffering completely ceases.
The views “I existed in the past” and “I did not exist,” and the views that the world is permanent and so on, rest on the earlier end.

cmp.note: 「见解、看法」，没有褒贬。英文 views；罗什品名作「邪见」，加了「错误」的评价。
cmp.en: Dṛṣṭi, “view, opinion,” neutral in itself. The English says “views”; Kumārajīva titles the chapter 邪见 (xiéjiàn, “wrong views”), adding a verdict.

verses.en: The views “I will not exist in the future,” “will I be someone else?”, and “I will exist,” and those about the world having an end and so on, rest on the later end.

cmp.note: 问的是「我将来存不存在」。英文 I will exist 照译；罗什「为作为不作」字面像是问「有没有作为」。
cmp.en: The question is “will I exist in the future?” The English “I will exist” follows it; Kumārajīva's 为作为不作 literally reads like “will I act or not act?”

verses.en: To say “I existed in the past” makes no sense. For whoever existed in former lives is not this very one.
If you say the self is the same, still what is grasped is different. Apart from what is grasped, which one is your self?

cmp.note: 这里指「被执取的东西」，即五蕴。英文 what is grasped 保持全书的 grasp 一族；罗什这几颂译「身」，更具体也更窄。
cmp.en: Here upādāna means “what is grasped,” the aggregates. The English keeps the book's “grasp” family with “what is grasped”; Kumārajīva renders it 身 (shēn, “body”) in these verses, more concrete and narrower.

verses.en: If you hold that there is no self apart from what is grasped, then the self would be just what is grasped — and yet you say there is no self.

cmp.note: 后半句 nāsti cātmeti vaḥ punaḥ「而你们又说没有自我」很简略，意思大致是「这样自我就等于不存在」。英文照字面。
cmp.en: The last phrase, “and yet you say there is no self,” is terse; the sense is roughly “then the self amounts to nothing.” The English stays literal.

verses.en: But what is grasped is not the self: it passes away and it arises. How can what is grasped be the one who grasps?
Nor does it make sense for the self to be other than what is grasped. If it were other, it would be perceived without anything grasped, yet it is not perceived.
So it is not other than what is grasped, nor is it just what is grasped. The self is not without what is grasped, nor is it simply nonexistent: this is the settled conclusion.
To say “I did not exist in the past” makes no sense either. For whoever existed in former lives is not someone other than this one.
If this one were someone else, he would exist even if that one were set aside. That one would stay just where he was, and this one would be born there without having died.

cmp.note: 「没有死就投生」。英文和白话译出；罗什「今我自生」没有「未死」这一层。
cmp.en: “Would be born without having died.” The English and plain Chinese keep it; Kumārajīva's 今我自生 (“the present I arises by itself”) loses “without having died.”

verses.en: There would be annihilation, the loss of karma; one person would experience karma done by another — these and other faults would follow.
Nor did it come into being without having existed before, for faults follow here too: the self would be something made, or something that came about without a cause.
So the views about the past — “I did not exist,” “I existed,” “both,” “neither” — make no sense.
The views about the future — “will I exist?” and “I will not exist” — are just like those about the past.
If that god were this human, it would be permanence. And the god would be unborn, since what is permanent is not born.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「这就是常」。英文 it would be permanence 照译；罗什加了「堕于常边」，点明是一种极端。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit just says “this is permanence.” The English follows it; Kumārajīva adds 堕于常边 (“falls into the extreme of permanence”).

verses.en: If the human were different from the god, it would be impermanence. If the human were different from the god, continuity would make no sense.
If one part were divine and one part human, it would be both impermanent and permanent, and that makes no sense.
If both impermanent and permanent were established, then you could grant that neither permanent nor impermanent is established too.
If someone came from somewhere and went on again to somewhere, then samsara would be without beginning. But there is no such someone.

cmp.note: 「某个人」：一个从某处来、到某处去的固定主体。英文 someone；罗什「法若定有来」换成了「法」。
cmp.en: “Someone”: a fixed subject who comes from somewhere and goes somewhere. The English says “someone”; Kumārajīva changes it to 法 (fǎ, “a dharma, a thing”).

verses.en: If nothing is permanent, what will be impermanent, or both permanent and impermanent, or set apart from both of these?
If the world had an end, how could there be another world? And if the world had no end, how could there be another world?
Since this continuum of the aggregates is like the flame of a lamp, neither having no end nor having an end makes sense.
If the earlier aggregates were destroyed and the later aggregates, depending on these, did not arise, then the world would have an end.
If the earlier aggregates were not destroyed and the later aggregates, depending on these, did not arise, then the world would have no end.

cmp.note: 罗什本这里多一颂「真法及说者，听者难得故……」，梵本没有。英文照梵本。
cmp.en: Kumārajīva adds an extra verse here (“because the true Dharma, its teachers and its hearers are hard to find…”) that the Sanskrit lacks. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: If one part had an end and one part had no end, the world would both have an end and have no end, and that makes no sense.
How could one part of the grasper perish while one part does not perish? That makes no sense.
And how could one part of what is grasped perish while one part does not perish? That makes no sense either.
If both having an end and having no end were established, then you could grant that neither having an end nor having no end is established too.
Or rather, since all things are empty, where, for whom, which, and from what would views like permanence arise?
I bow to Gautama, who out of compassion taught the true Dharma for the abandoning of all views.

cmp.note: 梵文只有佛的姓「乔达摩」。英文照译；罗什加了尊称「大圣主」。这一颂和第 1 品归敬颂首尾呼应：开头礼敬讲缘起的佛，结尾礼敬为断一切见而说法的佛。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit gives only the Buddha's family name, Gautama. The English follows it; Kumārajīva adds the honorific 大圣主 (“great holy lord”). This verse mirrors the opening homage of chapter 1: the book begins by bowing to the Buddha who taught dependent arising and ends by bowing to the Buddha who taught for the abandoning of all views.
